title: Generalised LQD tail exponents
lede: One exponent per side moves each LQD tail from exponential to Gaussian decay. The quoted strikes barely see it; the moments and the far wings do.
eq_labels: 1 · Quantile speed: slide 14's $e^{g}$ times one gauge per side
2 · Right tail of $X$, to leading order as $x \to \infty$ (the left mirrors it with $A_L$, $\alpha_-$)
3 · Far right wing of total variance, for $\alpha_+ > 0$
eq_note: $g$, $A_L = e^{g(0)}$, $A_R = e^{g(1)}$: as on slide 14. The gauge $1 - \log u$ grows like $1 + |z|$ in the left tail and tends to 1 in the right; $1 - \log(1-u)$ does the reverse, so each exponent acts on its own tail. $w(k)$: total implied variance at log-moneyness $k$. $\sim$: the ratio tends to one.
paras: Policy
one pair $(\alpha_-, \alpha_+)$ per underlying, shared by all its expiries and fixed before the fit. The default $\alpha_\pm = 0$ reproduces the exponential model bit for bit.
Why $\alpha$ is not fitted
a small $\alpha > 0$ moves the quoted smile by a few bp but makes every moment finite. The quotes cannot choose the class: compare scenarios instead.

head: $\alpha$ · preset
Log-return tail (right side)
Far-wing total variance
rows: Linear in $k$, at the Lee slope of the next slide
Gaussian rate, $e^{-x^2/(4A_R^2)}$: a normal tail of variance $2A_R^2$
Tends to the constant $2A_R^2$; Lee slope 0

example: AAPL 18-Sep-26 (0.17 y), same quotes, refitted with $\alpha_\pm = 0$ and with $\alpha_\pm = 1/2$: strip RMS 12.6 vs 12.5 vol bp, var-swap vol 32.06% vs 32.01%. The moments $\mathbb{E}[Y^r]$ are finite only for $-3.95 < r < 19.0$ at $\alpha = 0$, for every $r$ at $\alpha = 1/2$.
notes: Two slides back, the LQD law was built with exponential tails. This slide adds the one extension to that construction: a tail exponent on each side. The slide writes them alpha with a minus and alpha with a plus; call them the left exponent and the right exponent. Each sits between zero and one half.

The first line is the quantile's speed. The rank is u, and z is its log-odds, the log of u over one minus u. The speed of the quantile in z is the exponential of g, as before. It is multiplied by two gauges. The left gauge is one minus the log of u, raised to minus the left exponent. The right gauge is one minus the log of one minus u, raised to minus the right exponent. Each gauge is about one plus the size of z in its own tail, and tends to one in the other tail. So each exponent slows only its own tail. At exponent zero both gauges are one, and the law is the earlier one, exactly. The app skips the multiplication in that case, so default fits are bit-identical.

The second line is what the slowdown does to the log-return. Integrate the speed: the quantile grows like z to the power one minus alpha, instead of linearly. Invert that, and the log-probability of a return above x falls like minus a power of a ratio. The ratio is one minus alpha, times x, over the right tail scale; the power is one over one minus alpha. At alpha zero that is the exponential tail: the exponential of minus x over the tail scale. At one quarter the power is four thirds. At one half the power is two. That is the Gaussian rate, the tail of a normal law whose variance is twice the squared tail scale. These are leading-order statements, reached far out in the tail.

The third line is what it does to the smile far out. Total variance grows like k to a power: one minus two alpha, over one minus alpha. That is linear at alpha zero, k to the two thirds at one quarter, and flat at one half, where it tends to twice the squared tail scale. So any positive alpha gives a Lee slope of zero on that side, because every moment is finite there. The table lists the three presets of the panel: Exp, Int and Gauss.

The Gaussian rate describes the far tail only. The body is still the Legendre expansion of g, and it can be skewed or bimodal. A zero limiting slope does not mean a flat smile at traded strikes either. The wing can be steep over the quoted range and bend only far beyond it.

Policy. The exponents are chosen, not fitted. One pair per underlying, shared by every expiry of that underlying, set in the Options panel globally or per ticker. They sit beside the parameter vector, not inside it. So priors, the filter and the graph see the same number of parameters whatever the exponent.

Why not fit them. A small positive alpha is almost invisible on a finite strike strip, yet it changes the moment domain from finite up to some order to finite at every order. The strip is a recorded scenario run on AAPL, the September expiry. Refitted with Gaussian-rate tails on both sides, the strip error moves from 12.6 to 12.5 vol basis points, and the var-swap vol from 32.06 to 32.01 percent. But at alpha zero the moments of Y are finite only for orders between minus 3.95 and 19. At one half, all of them are. Same quotes, same fit quality, a different tail class. The desk makes that choice, and the scenario report compares its consequences.
Transition: the next slide makes the link between tails and wings exact, for any model: Lee's moment formula.

If asked why the range stops at one half: from zero to one half the family runs from the exponential class to the Gaussian rate. Beyond one half the exponent in the third line turns negative, so far-wing total variance would fall towards zero: tails thinner than Gaussian. The app rejects any value outside zero to one half.

If asked what replaces the condition that the right tail scale be below one: with a positive right exponent the forward is finite for any tail scale. What remains is a numerical guard at the edge of the grid, where z equals 40. The speed there is the tail scale times 41 to the power minus the right exponent, and it must stay below 0.999. At exponent one half that allows a tail scale up to about 6.4.

If asked how the exponents interact with calendar order: with a common exponent, the far expiry's tail scales must be at least the near one's, on each side. The calendar certificate, later in this section, reports that clause. Different exponents across expiries are outside the policy: a lighter far tail cannot be repaired by any fit.

title: Wing slopes and finite moments
lede: How steeply total variance grows in the far wings is set by how many moments the terminal price has. Lee's formula makes the link exact, for any model.
eq_labels: 1 · Wing slopes: growth of total variance per unit of $|k|$, far out
2 · Critical moments: how far the moments of $Y$ stay finite
3 · Lee's moment formula
4 · LQD with exponential tails: read off the tail scales
paras: Reading $\psi$

it falls from $\psi(0) = 2$, only the mean finite, to $0$ as $p \to \infty$: $\psi(1) = 0.34$, $\psi(16.9) = 0.029$. More finite moments, flatter wing. Inverse: $p = \frac{1}{2\beta} + \frac{\beta}{8} - \frac{1}{2}$.
In the app

LQD slopes come from $A_L$, $A_R$, and $A_R < 1$ keeps $\beta_R < 2$. The default SVI chart keeps both slopes below $1.95$; MCS reports its slopes and caps them at $1.95$ only in its structural chart.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Terminal price over the forward; its mean is one
Right (call) and left (put) wing slopes of $w$; always between 0 and 2
Right critical moment: $\mathbb{E}[Y^{1+p}]$ finite for $p < p^*$. The count starts after the mean, which is always finite
Left critical moment: $\mathbb{E}[Y^{-q}]$ finite for $q < q^*$; small when much probability sits near $Y = 0$
Lee's map from a critical moment to a wing slope
LQD tail scales (slide 14): $\mathbb{P}(X<x) \asymp e^{x/A_L}$, $\mathbb{P}(X>x) \asymp e^{-x/A_R}$, $X = \log Y$

example: Fit diagnostics: $A_L = 0.628$, $A_R = 0.056$. Left: $q^* = 1/0.628 = 1.59$, $\beta_L = \psi(1.59) = 0.243$. Right: $p^* = 1/0.056 - 1 = 16.9$, $\beta_R = \psi(16.9) = 0.029$. These are the card's Lee slopes: a steep put wing, a nearly flat call wing.
notes: The previous slide chose the tail class. This one connects the tail to something visible in the smile: how fast total variance grows in the far wings.

Notation first. Y is the terminal price divided by the forward, so its mean is one. k is log-moneyness, the log of strike over forward, and w of k is the total implied variance there: sigma squared times tau. The right wing slope, beta with an R on the slide, is the call side: far out, how much total variance grows per unit of k. The left wing slope is the same on the put side, per unit of minus k. The first line defines them as a limsup, the limit of the upper envelope, so they exist for any smile.

The second line is the critical moments. The right critical moment, p star on the slide, measures the right tail: the moments of Y of order one plus p stay finite for p below it. The count starts from one because the first moment, the forward, is always finite. The left critical moment, q star, measures the left tail through negative moments, Y to the minus q. Those blow up when much probability sits near zero.

The third line is Lee's theorem: each wing slope is psi of the critical moment on its side. Psi falls from 2 at p equal to zero, where only the mean is finite, to zero as p goes to infinity, where every moment is. At p equal to one it is 0.34. A heavy tail forces a steep wing; a light tail, a flat one. The ceiling of 2 is model-free. A steeper wing would price far out-of-the-money calls that never become worthless.

The fourth line is the LQD case, and it takes two lines of algebra. The right tail falls like the exponential of minus x over the right tail scale. Y to the power one plus p is the exponential of one plus p times x. So the moment is finite exactly when one plus p is below one over the tail scale. The right critical moment is one over the right tail scale, minus one. On the left, Y to the minus q is the exponential of minus q x, against a tail like the exponential of x over the left tail scale. So the left critical moment is one over the left tail scale. That is where the minus one on the right comes from, and why there is none on the left.

The strip is a recorded fit: QQQ, the December expiry, on 24 September. The tail scales are 0.628 on the left and 0.056 on the right. On the left, the critical moment is 1.59, and psi of that is 0.243. On the right, the critical moment is 16.9, and psi is 0.029. These are the Lee slopes the fit diagnostics card prints. Far out, the put wing gains about a quarter of a unit of total variance per unit of log-strike, and the call wing is almost flat.

What the app does with it. LQD needs no constraint: its slopes follow from the tail scales, and a right tail scale below one, which is the finite-forward condition, keeps the right slope below 2. SVI, in its default structural chart, holds both slopes below a cap of 1.95, strictly inside the ceiling, because a wing sitting exactly at 2 already misprices. MCS in its default chart has no cap. Its slopes are reported, and Quality flags any above 2. Its structural chart, which is opt-in, applies the same 1.95 cap.

Keep the scope in mind: these are limits. They say nothing about the shape just beyond the last quote, where options still carry value. That region has its own butterfly and calendar checks on the extrapolated wing.
Transition: the wings are also where a variance swap takes part of its value. Next slide.

If asked about the generalised tails: any positive exponent makes every moment finite on that side. So the critical moment is infinite and the Lee slope is zero, whatever the tail scale. The wing still grows, but slower than linearly.

If asked why 2 is the ceiling: take a ray where total variance equals beta times k, with beta above 2. Along it the Black call tends to one instead of zero as the strike goes to infinity. No law with a finite mean can produce that. At exactly 2 it tends to one half, still inadmissible; hence caps strictly below 2.
demo: Parametric ▸ Fit diagnostics ▸ wings · Lee · var-swap: $A_L$, $A_R$ and both slopes. Compare shows Lee L/R per model; Quality flags a slope above 2.

title: Variance swaps as an integrated constraint
lede: A variance-swap quote is one number per node, but it prices the whole strike strip, wings included. The fit meets it through one extra least-squares row.
eq_title: One node: $x = K/F$, log-return $X = \log(S_T/F_T)$, variance clock $\tau$
eq_labels: 1 · Fair total variance: the log contract, replicated with out-of-the-money options
2 · The objective as the solver sees it: a plain sum of squared rows (plus the model's penalty rows)
3 · The weight of the var-swap row: a share of the node's option weight
eq_note: $c(x)$, $p(x)$: undiscounted call and put in forward units. $\sigma_{\mathrm{VS}}^{\mathrm{quote}}$: the level on the card; $\sigma_{\mathrm{VS}}^{\mathrm{model}}$: the slice's own. $r_i$, $\lambda_i$: option residuals (vol units) and weights, slides 10 and 12. pct: the weight setting varSwapWeightPct, 10 by default.
paras: Why $\sqrt{\lambda}$

the solver only squares its rows and adds them up. A row $\sqrt{\lambda}\,e$ squares to $\lambda e^2$, so $\lambda$ is the weight of the miss $e$ in the objective. Weights add up across rows, which is why the setting is a share of $\sum_i\lambda_i$.
Why a share
10% means the same on a 20-quote node and on a 200-quote node. At 100% the single quote weighs as much as all the options together.
alt: Archived variance-swap card: model 25.03%, quote 25.04%, penalty 15% of quote weight, replication split, Hard pin switch
caption: QQQ 18-Dec-26, 24 September capture: quote 25.04%, model 25.03%. Weight 15% of the quote weight (default 10%), about 1% of the node's squared error. Replication: 87% from the quoted strikes, 13% from the put wing beyond them.
example: 225 quotes at equal weight: $\sum_i\lambda_i = 225$. Saved setting 15%: $\lambda_{\mathrm{VS}} = 0.15 \times 225 = 33.75$ (the card's 33.8), $\sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{VS}}} = 5.81$. The model misses the quote by about 1 vol bp, so the row reads about 5.8 bp; squared, it weighs as much as 33.75 option quotes each 1 bp off.
notes: A variance swap pays realised variance against a fixed strike. Its fair strike is one number per node, but it depends on the whole smile, wings included: exactly the part the option quotes leave free. A quote on it is new information.

The first line. x is strike over forward; p and c are the undiscounted put and call in forward units. The fair total variance is twice the integral of the out-of-the-money options, weighted by one over x squared: puts below the forward, calls above. That is the static replication of the log contract, so it equals minus two times the expected log-return. Divide by the variance clock tau and take the square root: that is the var-swap vol. It equals expected realised variance only for continuous paths. Jumps add a cubic correction, and discrete dividends sit outside the derivation. The fit uses this diffusion fair strike.

Each model evaluates the first line where it is cheapest. LQD takes minus two times the expected log-return straight from its quantile grid, with an analytic derivative. SVI and MCS integrate their closed-form smile on a fixed strike grid. Local volatility uses the same static replication, or optionally a backward PDE for the expected remaining variance.

The second line answers a question: why a weight lambda, and why its square root. The least-squares solver never sees weights. It squares its rows and adds them up. A var-swap miss should count with the var-swap weight. So the row given to the solver is the square root of that weight, times the miss. Squared, it gives back the weight times the squared miss. Every option row is built the same way: the square root of the quote's weight, times its residual. So the sum is exactly the weighted objective from the calibration slides, plus one term. The row is in vol units like the option rows. A one-basis-point var-swap miss trades against one-bp quote misses at the ratio of the weights, and nothing else.

Why the setting is the weight and not its square root: weights add up across rows, square roots do not. The third line makes the var-swap weight a percentage of the summed option weights. That is the setting varSwapWeightPct, 10 by default. At 100 percent the one var-swap quote weighs as much as all the options together. And that meaning does not depend on how many quotes the node has.

The strip is the recorded QQQ card. 225 quotes at equal weight, and a saved setting of 15 percent: the var-swap weight is 33.75, its square root 5.81. The model sits at 25.03 percent, the quote at 25.04. A miss of about one vol bp becomes a row of about 5.8 bp. Squared, it weighs like 33.75 option quotes each one bp off. The card reports the term as about 1 percent of the node's squared error.

Hard pin replaces the percentage by ten thousand times the option weight. In row units that is a hundred times the whole data block, so the fitted var-swap lands on the quote to solver tolerance. It is still a penalty, not an exact constraint. It stays below the weight of the calendar rows, so a pinned quote cannot override them. And prior var-swap rows are never pinned.

Where the response goes. One integrated number cannot say which wing should move. The caption's split shows the stake on this node: 87 percent of the replicated variance comes from the quoted strikes, 13 percent from the put wing beyond them. The model's own tail law decides how the pull is shared. So after a change, read both the remaining gap and the wings.
Transition: next, the second constraint that couples smiles: calendar order between expiries.

If asked how the local-volatility fit applies the same weight: its var-swap row is written in total variance, so the weight enters as a tolerance. The tolerance is two times the var-swap vol times tau, times one vol point, divided by the square root of the var-swap weight. Squared, the row carries the same weight as here.

If asked about the clock: the app quotes vols on its variance clock tau, which is calendar years when no events are set. Total variance is the same on any clock. A quote made on another clock must be converted before it is entered.
demo: Parametric aside ▸ Variance swap card: add a quote at the model level, move it and watch the wings. The weight % sits in Options ▸ Calibration; Hard pin makes the row stiff.

title: Calendar consistency across expiries
lede: Two expiries can each be a valid law and still price a calendar spread below zero. The test compares calls at the same moneyness, or the LQD ledger at the same rank.
eq_title: Expiries $T_1 < T_2$, each normalised by its own forward: $Y_T = S_T/F_T$, $\mathbb{E}[Y_T] = 1$
eq_labels: 1 · Same log-moneyness $k$: calls in forward units, equivalently total variance
2 · Same rank $u$: the upper share $G$ of slide 15, called the ledger
3 · Why the two tests agree: each curve is an extremum over the other
eq: c_{T_2}(k)\ge c_{T_1}(k)\ \ \forall k\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_{T_2}(k)\ge w_{T_1}(k)\ \ \forall k
eq_note: $c_T(k) = \mathbb{E}[(Y_T - e^{k})^+]$: call in forward units. $w_T(k)$: total implied variance at $k = \log(K/F_T)$. $Q_T$: quantile of $\log Y_T$ at rank $u$. $G_T(u)$: the share of the forward paid by the outcomes above the $u$-quantile, from $G_T(0) = 1$ down to $G_T(1) = 0$.
paras: Convex order
equal means and ordered calls: the far law is a mean-preserving spread of the near one, and some martingale has both as marginals (Kellerer).
Variance, not vol
the order is on $w$. At the money, $(w_{T_2} - w_{T_1})/(T_2 - T_1)$ is the forward variance; the vol itself may fall with maturity.
alt: Reference figure: a far slice fitted alone lies below the near slice in total variance; refitted under a floor at the near slice, it is lifted onto the near curve
caption: Reference-note figure: total variance against $k$, near $T = 0.25$ (grey, under the teal), far $T = 0.5$. Fitted alone, the far slice (red, dashed) lies below the near one: negative forward variance across the shaded range. Refitted under a floor at the near slice (teal), it is lifted onto the near curve and no further.
example: The figure's pair at the money: 3 months at 30%, $w = 0.0225$; 6 months at 20%, $w = 0.0200$. Forward variance $(0.0200 - 0.0225)/0.25 = -0.010$: an arbitrage. With 24% at 3 months ($w = 0.0144$), 20% at 6 months is fine: forward vol 15.0%.
reference: Note 10 · Note 01 §11 · convex order under deterministic carry
notes: Two expiries of the same underlying, each fitted well on its own, can still disagree with each other. Together they can price a calendar spread below zero. This slide is the test; the next one is the repair.

Notation. The near expiry and the far expiry are the subscripts one and two on the slide. Each is normalised by its own forward: the terminal price over the forward, with mean one. The call in forward units at log-moneyness k is c of k, and w of k is the total implied variance there. The upper share, G of u, is the quantity from the LQD slides that the app calls the ledger: the share of the forward paid by the outcomes above the u-quantile. It starts at one at rank zero, where every outcome counts, and falls to zero at rank one.

The first line is the condition. At every log-moneyness, the far call is worth at least the near call. Because the Black price rises with total variance at a fixed k, that is the same as the far total variance being at least the near one. With equal means, ordering every call orders every convex payoff. The far law is then a mean-preserving spread of the near one, which is convex order. By Kellerer's theorem, convex order plus a valid density at each date is exactly what it takes for some martingale to have these laws as its marginals.
The second line is the same order, read at the same rank instead of the same strike. The far ledger must lie above the near ledger at every rank.

The third line says why the two readings agree. Take the outcomes above rank u and pay the strike on that event. You collect the ledger at u, and you pay the exponential of k times one minus u. The best cut-off is the strike's own rank, so the call is the maximum of that difference over u. Read backwards, the ledger is a minimum over strikes. A maximum, or a minimum, of ordered curves is ordered. So order at every strike and order at every rank are the same statement. Comparing densities point by point would not be.

Why keep both readings. The quotes sit at strikes, so the fit is screened at fixed strikes on the common quote support. The rank reading is free for LQD, since the ledger is already computed for pricing, and it reaches the far tails without any implied-vol inversion. The certificate on the next slide uses it.

Variance, not vol. The strip takes the figure's pair at the money. Three months at 30 percent is a total variance of 0.0225. Six months at 20 percent is 0.02. The far total variance is lower, so the forward variance is negative, minus 0.01: a calendar spread with a negative price. For this pair to be admissible the six-month vol needs at least 21.2 percent. Now put the three-month vol at 24 percent. Its total variance is 0.0144, and the same 20 percent at six months is fine, with a forward variance of 0.0224 and a forward vol of 15 percent. A vol that falls with maturity is not the problem. A total variance that falls is.

The figure is a reference example. Fitted alone, the far slice sits below the near one across the whole strip. Refitted under a floor at the near slice, it is lifted onto the near curve and no further: zero forward variance there, the edge of what is admissible. In this figure only the far slice moves. The production repair on the next slide lets both move.
Transition: how the app finds and repairs such a pair, and how it proves the result: next slide.

If asked about dividends and rates: the comparison is at fixed forward moneyness, under deterministic carry. At a fixed cash strike, with discrete dividends, raw prices can cross without any arbitrage. Stochastic rates would break the equivalence altogether.

If asked about local volatility: a positive local variance makes Dupire prices increase with maturity at every strike, so calendar order holds by construction. The app only checks the discrete scheme.

title: Calendar repair and numerical certification
lede: Fit each expiry alone, repair only the pairs that violate, then certify the stored surface on the whole line: at the nodes, between them and in the tails.
eq_title: Adjacent expiries near and far, on the log-odds grid $z_j = -40 + j\,h$, $h = 0.01$
eq_labels: 1 · Ledger gap at the same rank, and its exact slope at every node
2 · Hermite ledger gap: on each cell, the cubic that matches both end values and both end slopes
3 · Interior candidates: where that cubic's slope vanishes
4 · Certificate: the minimum over nodes, interior roots and one tail point per side
eq_note: $G(z)$: the ledger of slide 23 at rank $u = 1/(1+e^{-z})$; $Q_{\mathrm{near}}$, $Q_{\mathrm{far}}$: the two quantiles. With $d = \Delta G(z_{j+1}) - \Delta G(z_j)$, $m_0 = h\,\partial_z\Delta G(z_j)$, $m_1 = h\,\partial_z\Delta G(z_{j+1})$: $c_0 = \Delta G(z_j)$, $c_1 = m_0$, $c_2 = 3d - 2m_0 - m_1$, $c_3 = m_0 + m_1 - 2d$. Grid: 8,001 nodes, $|z| \le 40$. Tolerance $10^{-6}$ of the forward, 0.01 bp.
paras: Why exact
the pricer reads the same Hermite cubics, so this minimum is the minimum of the stored surface, not a sample. A node-only check can miss a dip inside a cell (strip).
Tails
beyond $|z| = 40$ both ledgers follow their tail continuations: one closed-form candidate per side. Tail order, far scales $\ge$ near ones, is a separate clause.

head: Step
Calculation
Outcome
rows: Each expiry on its own quotes, no calendar rows
A clean ladder keeps them, bit for bit
Near minus far call on the common quote support, over vega
Joint Gauss–Newton on each violating run; hinge weight $\times 10$, at most 3 times
Both slices concede, by their data weight
Where the certificate fails: stiff ledger row ($10^6$) at the worst rank; refit
Exact minimum of the Hermite ledger gap
Far tail scales $\ge$ near ones, on each side
Advisory; blocks only with the Tail-order gate

example: One cell, $h = 0.01$: gap $2\times10^{-6}$ at both nodes, slopes $\mp 0.002$. The cubic is $\Delta\hat G = 2\cdot10^{-6}\,(1 - 10t + 10t^2)$; its slope vanishes at $t = 1/2$, where $\Delta\hat G = -3\times10^{-6}$. Both nodes pass the $-10^{-6}$ tolerance; the cell fails.
reference: Calendar roadmap phases 0 and 4 · calib/symmetric.py · symmetric_exchange.py · calendar_certificate.py
notes: The previous slide gave the test. This one shows how the app enforces it, then proves the result, and it defines the Hermite ledger gap. Start with the table, top to bottom.

Step one: fit every expiry on its own quotes, with no calendar rows. Step two is the screen. For each adjacent pair, compare near and far calls at fixed strikes, on the strikes both expiries quote, divided by vega so the number reads as a vol gap. Above half a vol basis point it is a violation. Most ladders are clean, and then the independent fits are kept, bit for bit.

Step three is the symmetric repair. Each run of violating pairs is refitted jointly by Gauss–Newton, a least-squares solver that linearises the residuals at each step. The rows are both slices' own quote rows, plus hinge rows on the interface. Each slice keeps its quote weights, so the better-informed slice moves less. If a violation survives, the hinge weight is multiplied by ten, at most three times. The older sequential route, near to far with each slice floored by the previous one, made the later expiry pay for everything.

Step four is the exchange. Any pair the certificate still rejects gets a stiff ledger row, weight one million, at the rank where the certificate found its worst gap, and is refitted. Up to eight rounds. A pair whose worst rank keeps coming back is declared irreducible: its quotes disagree, and the app reports it rather than flattening the surface.

Now the certificate, and the term in the title. The first line is the ledger gap: the far ledger minus the near ledger at the same rank, the previous slide's comparison, written on the log-odds grid. That grid has 8,001 nodes from minus 40 to 40, step 0.01. The gap's slope is known exactly at every node: u times one minus u, times the exponential of the near quantile minus the exponential of the far quantile. So the gap can only turn where the two quantile curves cross.

The second line is the Hermite ledger gap. Between nodes, the app stores each ledger as a cubic Hermite interpolant. On every cell, that is the one cubic that matches the exact values and the exact slopes at both ends; Hermite interpolation means matching slopes as well as values. The pricer reads call prices from that same interpolant. The Hermite ledger gap is the difference of the two stored cubics: one cubic per cell again, with the four coefficients listed under the formulas.

The third line. On a cell, a cubic reaches its minimum at an end or where its slope is zero, and the slope is a quadratic in t. So the candidates are finite: every node, at most two roots per cell, and beyond the grid one closed-form point per side, where the two tail continuations cross. The fourth line is the certificate. It takes the minimum over all of them and requires it above minus ten to the minus six, a hundredth of a basis point of the forward. It is the minimum of the stored object, not of a sample, so it is exact.

The strip shows why the interior roots matter. One cell: the gap is plus two times ten to the minus six at both nodes, with slopes minus and plus 0.002. The cubic is two times ten to the minus six, times one minus ten t plus ten t squared. Its slope vanishes in the middle, where the gap is minus three times ten to the minus six. Both nodes pass, the cell fails. A check at the nodes alone would accept it.

The last row is the tail order. With common tail exponents, each far tail scale must be at least the near one, so the far law never has a lighter tail. It is reported and advisory by default; the Tail-order gate option makes it block. Policy overall: a failed certificate takes the node out of ready and blocks Publish, and the Quality card names the gap in bp and its strike.
Transition: that completes the parametric surface. Next, local volatility, where calendar order holds by construction and the work is in the fit itself.

If asked why the exchange uses ledger rows when the screen uses prices: a floor on the whole ledger drags a fit by its unquoted tails. The ledger at one rank integrates everything above it. That is why the screen and the repair work at quoted strikes. The exchange adds a ledger row only at the few ranks the certificate rejects.

title: A piecewise-affine local-variance surface
lede: The local-volatility fit has one unknown per vertex of a strike–time grid: the local variance there. Between vertices the surface is affine on triangles, so positive vertices give a positive surface.
eq_title: Local variance $\nu(\tau,x)$ at normalised strike $x = K/F$ and variance time $\tau$
eq_labels: 1 · One unknown per vertex, one hat function per unknown
2 · Inside a triangle: an average of its three corners
3 · So a box on the vertices is a box on the whole surface
eq_note: $\phi_\ell$: hat function of vertex $(\tau_\ell, x_\ell)$, 1 there, 0 at every other vertex, affine on each triangle. $m = n_\tau n_x$ vertices; each grid rectangle is cut into two triangles. $b_a$: barycentric weights of $(\tau, x)$ in its triangle, with corners $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$.
paras: Not an implied vol
a price averages local variance along the paths to expiry; at the money, $\sigma_{\mathrm{ATM}}^2(\tau) \approx \frac1\tau\int_0^\tau \nu(s,1)\,ds$. A vertex is read through the pricing equation.
Vertices
time rows at $0$, $\tau_1/4$ and each expiry, at least 10; strike columns on a delta axis in the quoted range, at least 12, and 8 inside each expiry's range.
Outside the grid
flat on the right. On the left flat by default, or linear at $a$ times the first cell's slope with Convex wing ($a = 1.5$) or a variance-swap quote ($a$ fitted).
alt: Archived local-variance mesh fitted across QQQ expiries
caption: 24 September capture of the fitted QQQ sheet: $11 \times 28$ vertices, time rows by strike columns. Each facet is a triangle on which $\nu$ is affine; height and colour give the local variance, $0.0025$ to $1.44$. STALE refers to the saved snapshot.
example: Weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 on corners at 20%, 30%, 25% local vol: $\nu = 0.5(0.04) + 0.3(0.09) + 0.2(0.0625) = 0.0595$, a local vol of 24.4%. Variances are averaged, not vols, and the result stays between 20% and 30%.
notes: This section changes the object. Until now each expiry had its own smile model. Local volatility describes the whole surface with one diffusion. The forward-normalised price moves with an instantaneous variance, nu, that depends on where it is, x, and when, tau. x is the normalised strike, strike over forward. tau is the variance clock: calendar time plus any event days, and equal to calendar time when no events are set. Nu is a variance, local vol squared.

The first line. The unknowns are a finite list of numbers, one per vertex of a grid in time and strike. Each unknown, theta on the slide, is the local variance at its vertex. Between vertices the surface is built from hat functions. A hat function equals one at its own vertex, zero at every other vertex, and is affine on each triangle. The grid is a tensor product, time rows by strike columns, and each rectangle is cut into two triangles. The QQQ sheet in the capture has 11 time rows and 28 strike columns: 308 numbers describe the whole surface. The chart labels its time axis T; it is the variance clock tau.

The second line is the key property. A point inside a triangle takes the weighted average of the triangle's three corner values, with barycentric weights: nonnegative, summing to one. An average cannot leave the range of what it averages. The strip: weights of one half, 0.3 and 0.2 on corners at 20, 30 and 25 percent local vol give a variance of 0.0595, a local vol of 24.4 percent. Variances are averaged, not vols.

The third line follows at once. Bounds on the vertices are bounds on the whole surface inside the grid. So positivity, the condition that makes the diffusion exist and its prices free of arbitrage, is a box on each unknown. A least-squares solver handles a box directly, with no penalty. The cap is 60 percent vol, or three times the highest quoted implied vol if that is larger, and never above 400 percent. The floor is 5 percent vol, lowered to half the lowest at-the-money implied vol when that is smaller.

Why the floor may sit below every implied vol. An option's implied variance is an average of local variance along the paths to its expiry. At the money, roughly, the implied variance to tau is the time average of the at-the-money local variance up to tau. When the term structure rises, the early local variance must sit below the shortest implied variance. The same fact is the first bullet: a vertex value is not the implied vol of an option at that point. It is read through the pricing equation, which is the next slide.

Where the vertices go. Time rows sit at zero, at a quarter of the first expiry and at every expiry. Then the widest gaps, measured in square-root time, are split until there are at least ten rows after zero. Strike columns come from a delta axis: the 1, 2, 5, 10, 25 and 40 delta points of each side, plus the money. They are scaled by the longest expiry and clipped to the quoted range. There are at least twelve, and at least eight inside each expiry's own quoted range. That last rule exists because a six-day weekly once caught only three vertices on its smile and fitted at 108 basis points. With eight it came down to about 28.

Outside the grid. To the right, the local variance is held flat at its last column. To the left it is flat by default. With the Convex wing option it continues linearly at 1.5 times the slope of the first cell. With a variance-swap quote that multiple becomes a fitted parameter between 0 and 20. There the averaging argument no longer holds, so a falling continuation could turn negative; the march floors it at zero.
Transition: next, how a sheet of local variance becomes option prices: the forward Dupire march.

If asked why triangles rather than bilinear cells: on a triangle the interpolant is exactly affine and is fixed by its three corners. That also works on vertex sets that are not rectangular. Bilinear cells keep the averaging property but add a cross term. The diagonal of each rectangle comes from the triangulation's tie-break rule, and the viewer draws the triangulation the pricing uses.

If asked why the unknown is a variance rather than a vol: the pricing equation is linear in the local variance. So the derivative of the operator with respect to one vertex is exact and cheap, which the calibration, two slides ahead, uses. And averaging variances is what keeps the positivity argument.

If asked whether the sheet is unique: no. Prices average local variance, so different sheets can reprice the same quotes. Two recorded sheets sit 22 vol points apart in the unquoted deep-put wing and reprice the same quotes within 1.6 vol basis points. The regularisation in the calibration, two slides ahead, chooses one.
demo: Local Vol lens (Alt+4) ▸ LV surface: rotate the mesh. Options ▸ Local-Vol surface: the resolved grid $n_\tau \times n_x = m$ and the box.

title: The forward Dupire pricing calculation
lede: Given a local-variance sheet, one forward march prices every strike and every expiry: start from the payoff and step forward in time, one tridiagonal solve per step.
eq_title: Call over $DF$, $c(\tau,x)$, at normalised strike $x = K/F$; on the lattice, $U^n_i = c(\tau_n, x_i)$
eq_labels: 1 · Forward Dupire equation, started from the payoff
2 · Three-point stencil: row $i$ of the matrix $A$
3 · One BDF2 step: a single tridiagonal solve
4 · Step weights from the step ratio $\omega_n = \Delta\tau_n/\Delta\tau_{n-1}$
eq_note: Boundaries: $c(\tau,0) = 1$ and $c(\tau,x_{\max}) = 0$, with $x_{\max} = \max(1.4\,x_{\mathrm{top}},\ 2.5)$ and $x_{\mathrm{top}}$ the highest quoted strike. Step one, and any step more than twice the previous one, is implicit Euler: $(\gamma, \alpha, \beta) = (1, 1, 0)$.
paras: What BDF2 is

backward differentiation, order 2: the time derivative at $\tau_{n+1}$ is the slope of the parabola through $U^{n-1}$, $U^n$ and $U^{n+1}$, with $A$ taken at $\tau_{n+1}$. Error $O(\Delta\tau^2)$; the stiffest modes are damped to zero (L-stable), so the payoff kink does not ring.
Grids

strike step $0.15\,\sigma\sqrt\tau$ over each expiry's range $\pm6\sigma\sqrt\tau$, 0.02 in the wings, $x = 1$ a node. Time steps start at 1% of the first grid mark and grow by at most 25%, capped at 0.05; every expiry and vertex row is on the grid.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Call over $DF$, carry inside $F$ and $D$; local variance, the sheet of the previous slide
Variance time (slide 29): calendar time plus event days; $t$ itself with no events
Lattice node $i$; widths of the cells below ($h_i^-$) and above ($h_i^+$) it
$\nu(\tau_{n+1}, x_i)$; stencil weights $x_i^2/\bigl((h_i^-+h_i^+)\,h_i^\pm\bigr)$, the $\tfrac12$ folded in
Call values on the lattice at time level $\tau_n$
Step $\tau_{n+1}-\tau_n$; its ratio to the previous step
Step weights: implicit Euler $(1, 1, 0)$; constant-step BDF2 $(\tfrac23, \tfrac43, \tfrac13)$

example: A flat 15% sheet, whose exact price is known, marched over the SPY ladder of 23 September (2 to 359 days): 115 graded steps, the first 7 minutes long. ATM vol error: implicit Euler 16 bp at 2 days, 5 to 12 bp further out; BDF2 3.2 bp at 2 days, at most 0.3 bp further out.
notes: The first line is the forward Dupire equation. c is the call price divided by the discount factor and the forward, as a function of the normalised strike x, strike over forward, and of the variance time tau. Rates, dividends and borrow sit inside the forward and the discount factor, so they do not appear. The equation says the call gains value with maturity. The rate is one half the local variance, times x squared, times the convexity of the call in strike. That convexity is the risk-neutral density. It starts from the payoff, one minus x floored at zero. At x equal to zero the call is worth the whole forward, one. At the far edge it is worth zero; that edge is 1.4 times the highest quoted strike, and at least 2.5. Why forward: the Black–Scholes equation runs backward from one option's payoff, one solve per option. Dupire's runs forward in maturity with strike as the space variable. So one march produces the whole call surface, and every quote of every expiry is read off the same solution.

The second line is space. On the strike lattice the second derivative at node i uses node i and its two neighbours only. The widths of the cells below and above the node are the h with a minus and the h with a plus on the slide. The two stencil weights are the node's x squared, divided by the sum of the two widths and by the width on that side. The one half of the equation is already folded in. Multiply by the local variance at the node, taken at the new time level, and that is row i of the matrix A. Three entries per row: A is tridiagonal, which means each row touches only the diagonal and its two neighbours.

The third line is time, and this is BDF2. BDF stands for backward differentiation formula, and 2 is its order. Take the two last known time levels and the unknown new one. Draw the parabola through the three in time, and use its slope at the new time as the time derivative. Set that slope equal to A times the new level. At a constant step it reads: three times the new level, minus four times the current one, plus the previous one, over twice the step, equals A times the new level. Rearranged, that is the third line with gamma two thirds, alpha four thirds and beta one third. The fourth line gives the weights when the step length changes, through the ratio omega of this step to the last one. Alpha minus beta is always one, so a flat price stays flat.

What it buys. Implicit Euler, the legacy scheme, is first order: halve the step and you halve the error. BDF2 is second order: halve the step and you quarter it. And it is L-stable. The stiffest modes, the jagged strike-scale components the payoff kink injects, are damped to zero. Crank–Nicolson lets them flip sign at every step instead of dying, and that ringing, with negative densities, was recorded on coarse strike grids. BDF2 needs two past levels, so its first step is implicit Euler. So is any step more than twice the previous one, because variable-step BDF2 is only stable for growth below one plus root two. The graded grid never grows by more than 25 percent, so from step two on every step is BDF2.

The grids. In time: the payoff kink makes the at-the-money price grow like the square root of tau, so near zero the natural time scale is tau itself. Steps start at one percent of the first grid mark and grow geometrically by at most 25 percent, capped at 0.05 years, with at least eight steps between marks. Every expiry and every vertex row is a mark, because the local variance has a kink in time at each row. In strike: each expiry gets its own step, 0.15 of its at-the-money standard deviation, out to six standard deviations. The wings step 0.02, the step changes by at most 15 percent per cell, and x equal to one is always a node. For a two-day front at 15 percent vol that is a step of about one six-hundredth, between 0.94 and 1.07.

Positivity. The left-hand matrix is an M-matrix: positive diagonal, non-positive off-diagonals, diagonally dominant. So the solve needs no pivoting, and its inverse has no negative entry. The minus-beta term on the right means that alone does not prove the full two-level update keeps the density positive. So every fit measures it: the smallest second difference per expiry, calendar order and price bounds are checked on the output.

The strip. A flat 15 percent sheet has a known answer: 15 percent at every strike. Marched over the SPY ladder of 23 September, two to 359 days, the graded grid has 115 steps, the first one seven minutes long. Implicit Euler misses the at-the-money vol by 16 basis points at two days, and by 5 to 12 bp further out. BDF2 misses by 3.2 bp at two days, which is the strike lattice's share, and by at most 0.3 bp elsewhere. On fitted surfaces the recorded figure is at most about 5 bp per expiry for BDF2, where the old implicit rule left 15 to 170 bp for the fit to absorb.
Transition: the fit must now choose the sheet. Next, how the calibration differentiates this march, and why that stays cheap.

If asked what BDF2 is, in one sentence: an implicit two-step method that takes the time derivative from a parabola through the last three levels. It is second order like Crank–Nicolson, but it damps the stiff modes like implicit Euler.

If asked why not Crank–Nicolson: it is second order but not L-stable. Its amplification tends to minus one on the stiffest modes, so the payoff kink rings. And its sensitivity step costs more, up to about twice, because it also applies the operator to the old level. It stays available as Rannacher, which is Crank–Nicolson after two implicit start-up steps, as an option.

If asked how big the lattice is: for the SPY ladder of 23 September, 368 strike nodes and 116 time levels. The old uniform lattice took the shortest expiry's step everywhere. On a SPY surface with a two-day expiry, that was about 1,700 strike nodes where the graded one needs about 400.

title: Calibrating through the PDE
lede: The fit chooses the vertex values $\theta$ by damped Gauss–Newton. The derivatives it needs come out of the same march as the prices, through the same tridiagonal matrix.
eq_title: Unknowns $\theta$: the $m$ vertex variances; quotes $i = 1, \ldots, n$
eq_labels: 1 · Quote residual: the price miss over vega, in vol points
2 · Objective: weighted misses plus three penalties, minimised over the box $\nu_{\mathrm{lo}} \le \theta \le \nu_{\mathrm{hi}}$
3 · Sensitivities $S_\ell = \partial U/\partial\theta_\ell$: the same matrix, one more right-hand side each
4 · Levenberg–Marquardt step on the stacked residuals $r$, with $\|r\|^2 = \Phi$, clipped to the box
paras: Why tridiagonal
the second difference at node $i$ uses nodes $i-1$, $i$, $i+1$ only: three entries per row of $A$. One pivot-free factorisation per step, $O(N_x)$, serves the price and all $m$ columns $S_\ell$.
Gauss–Newton, Levenberg–Marquardt

linearise, $r(\theta+\Delta\theta) \approx r + J\Delta\theta$, and solve that least squares. The damping $\mu$ shortens the step toward the gradient: it falls after good steps, rises after rejected ones. LSMR needs only $Jv$ and $J^{\top}w$.
Regularisation

prices average local variance over paths, so many sheets fit the same quotes. The penalties pick one: least curvature, smoothest density, and early rows tied to the first expiry, which pins only their average.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Model call at quote $i$, read off the march; the market mid. Both over $DF$
Black vega of the quote, floored at $10^{-3}$; quote weight. A 1-point vol miss gives $r_i \approx 1$
Second differences of neighbouring vertices along strike and along time, spacing-aware: $\theta_{j-1}-2\theta_j+\theta_{j+1}$ on an even grid
Third differences of each expiry's marched call, the slope of the density $\partial_{xx}c$, over the quoted range $\pm2$ ATM std
Vertex rows at $\tau = 0$ and the next one; before a front under 0.08 y, every row up to it, at weight at least 1
Penalty weights, by default $10^{-2}$, $1$, $10^{-2}$ (Options: Roughness, Density smoothness, Front-tie weight)
$\partial A/\partial\theta_\ell$: $A$ with $\nu_i$ replaced by $\phi_\ell(\tau_{n+1}, x_i)$; $\gamma, \alpha, \beta$ as on slide 26
Jacobian of all rows of $r$, built from the $S_\ell$; damping, $10^{-3}$ at the start

example: 875 quotes, $m = 253$ vertices, lattice 368 strikes by 115 steps. One evaluation marches the price and up to 253 columns $S_\ell$: $115 \times 366 \times 253 \approx 10.6$ million node updates behind one factorisation per step. Cold fit: 66 evaluations, 2.8 s. Warm-started from the last fit: 20 evaluations, 0.9 s.
notes: This slide fits the sheet: choose the vertex variances, theta on the slide, so that the marched prices meet the quotes. The first line is the quote residual. The model call at quote i is read off the march; the other term is the market mid; both are divided by the discount factor and the forward. The miss is divided by 0.01 times the quote's Black vega, floored at ten to the minus three. So the residual reads in vol points: a one-point miss gives about one, a one-basis-point miss a hundredth. In bid–ask and haircut modes the band residual from the calibration section takes its place, with the same weak mid anchor.

The second line is the objective: the squared misses weighted by the quote weights, plus three penalties, over the box from two slides back. The first penalty is the curvature of the sheet; its weight is the Roughness setting, the first kappa on the slide. It is the second difference of neighbouring vertices, along strike within a time row and along time within a strike column, each scaled by the local spacing. On an even grid it is the left value, minus twice the middle, plus the right. The second penalty is the roughness of the density; its weight is the Density smoothness setting. It is the third difference of each expiry's marched call, which is the slope of the density, over its quoted range widened by two at-the-money standard deviations. It is scaled so that a smooth bell costs about 0.14 times its weight, whatever the maturity. The third penalty is the front tie; its weight is the Front-tie weight setting. It pulls the rows before the first expiry toward it. Defaults: 0.01, 1 and 0.01.

Why regularise at all. Prices are averages of local variance along the diffusion's paths, so the data leave some directions almost free: 253 unknowns against quotes packed near the money of nine expiries. Before the first expiry the quotes pin only the average of the local variance, not its shape. Beyond the quoted wings they pin almost nothing. Two recorded sheets sit 22 vol points apart in the unquoted put wing and reprice the same quotes within 1.6 vol basis points. The penalties choose one member of that family: the least curved sheet, the smoothest density, and a front that continues the first expiry. When the first expiry is under a month, the front tie is chained over every early row at weight one. Untied, those rows were measured ringing by 5 to 30 vol points.

How much they weigh. A one-bp miss costs ten to the minus four. A kink of 0.01 in variance between neighbouring vertices costs ten to the minus six. So the curvature penalty decides where the quotes are silent and yields where they speak. The density rows aim at what the quotes cannot see: vertex-scale ringing that shows up as spikes in the density. On the SPY weekly fixture they cut the finer-lattice RMS from 20.2 to 18.5 bp, and the evaluations from 62 to 43.

The third line is the derivatives. Differentiate the step of the previous slide with respect to one vertex. The left-hand matrix does not change. On the right, the previous sensitivities combine exactly like the prices, plus a source term: the stencil with the local variance replaced by that vertex's hat function, applied to the new prices. That is exact, because the equation is linear in the local variance. Read it as: a vertex moves prices only where the diffusion passes through its triangles, in proportion to the convexity it meets there.

Why a tridiagonal matrix, and why it matters. The second derivative at node i uses only the node and its two neighbours, so each row has three entries. Such a system is solved by one forward sweep and one back substitution, the Thomas algorithm, in a few operations per node. And because this matrix is an M-matrix, no pivoting is needed. Factor it once per step and reuse it for the price and for all 253 sensitivity columns. The compiled march keeps the columns as its inner loop, so the processor works on several columns per instruction.

The fourth line is the optimiser. Gauss–Newton replaces the residuals near the current point by their linearisation, the residual plus the Jacobian times the step, and solves that linear least-squares problem. The Jacobian, J on the slide, holds the derivative of every residual row, built from the sensitivities. Levenberg–Marquardt adds the damping, mu, scaled by the diagonal of the Gauss–Newton matrix, the product of the Jacobian's transpose with itself. A small mu gives the Gauss–Newton step; a large mu gives a short step down the scaled gradient. A trial is kept if the objective falls; mu shrinks after a good step and grows after a rejected one. The step is clipped to the box. In band modes the clipped vertices are pinned and the rest re-solved. The linear system is solved by LSMR, an iterative least-squares method that needs only products of the Jacobian, and of its transpose, with a vector. It never forms the Gauss–Newton matrix and never does a dense decomposition. The fit stops at convergence, at 200 evaluations, or when the quote misfit has not improved by 0.3 percent in 18 evaluations, 12 in band modes, and returns the best accepted point. Fits with a variance-swap quote use a trust-region solver instead.

The computational picture, the strip. SPY on 23 September: 875 quotes, 253 vertices, a lattice of 368 strikes by 115 steps. One evaluation marches the price and up to 253 sensitivity columns. That is 115 steps, times 366 interior nodes, times 253 columns: about 10.6 million node updates, behind one factorisation per step. A column stays zero until the march reaches its vertex's rows, so fewer are live on average. Measured today on a synthetic surface of that size, one such march takes about 17 milliseconds on this laptop. The recorded cold fit took 66 evaluations and 2.8 seconds. Warm-started from the previous fit, 20 evaluations and 0.9 seconds. Total time is the cost of one evaluation times the number of evaluations, and every speed-up attacked one of the two. The compiled march and the graded grids cut the first. The Dupire seed of a cold fit, the warm start and the early stop cut the second.
Transition: last slide of the section: the fitted sheet beside the local variance read directly off the parametric smiles.

If asked why a tridiagonal matrix: the equation has one space dimension, and its second derivative is approximated by a three-point stencil, so each unknown couples only to its two neighbours. That makes each step linear in the number of nodes, and lets one factorisation serve the price and every sensitivity.

If asked what Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt are: Gauss–Newton is Newton's method for least squares with the second derivatives of the residuals dropped. The Hessian is then replaced by the product of the Jacobian's transpose with itself. Levenberg–Marquardt adds a damping term that blends it with gradient descent and adapts from step to step: full steps near the answer, cautious ones far from it. The fit uses forward sensitivities rather than an adjoint because Gauss–Newton needs the whole Jacobian of 875 quote rows, not the gradient of one number.

title: Fitted local variance and the Dupire-derived surface
lede: The Compare tab reads a local variance off the parametric smiles the classical way, differentiate then divide, and scores it beside the fitted sheet on the same quotes.
eq_title: One equation, read in both directions
eq_labels: 1 · Dupire twin: differentiate the parametric surface, then divide
2 · Round trip: reprice the twin, compare it with its own source at the quoted $k_i$
eq_note: $w(k,\tau)$: the parametric total variance, interpolated in $\tau$ by a monotone cubic (Smooth) or linearly (Buckets). $g = \bigl(1-\frac{k\,\partial_k w}{2w}\bigr)^2-\frac{(\partial_k w)^2}{4}\bigl(\frac1w+\frac14\bigr)+\frac12\partial_{kk}w$, the butterfly function; cells with $g \le 0$ or $\partial_\tau w \le 0$ are counted as repairs. $\sigma_{\mathrm{twin}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{param}}$: implied vols of the repriced twin and of its source.
paras: Twin
repriced on the fit's lattice made four times finer in strike and eight times finer in time, second-order (Rannacher). Read-only: the tab never writes to the fit.
Affine
the direct fit of slides 25–27. rms: on its own lattice; conv: the same sheet repriced on a lattice twice as fine in strike and four times in time.
Controls
floor: a flat sheet through the twin's operator, whose error is the operator's own. sheet: the twin sampled at the fit's vertices and repriced, which is what the vertex grid loses.
alt: Archived comparison of parametric, Dupire-derived and directly fitted local-volatility smiles
caption: 24 September capture, QQQ 18-Dec-26, haircut target: affine sheet (blue), parametric source (green), Dupire twin (orange, dashed). Its row reads parametric 2, twin 4, affine 2 (conv 8) bp; round trip 0.3 bp over a floor of 0.1, while the twin sampled at the vertices reprices 71 bp away.
example: Nine expiries, 875 quotes, 253 vertices: 3.61 vol bp RMS on the fit's own lattice, 5.12 bp repriced on the finer one, 24.8 bp worst quote. Quote both: a fit can absorb its own lattice's error into $\theta$, and only another lattice shows it.
notes: The last three slides read Dupire's equation forward: choose a local variance, march the prices, match the quotes. The Compare tab reads it the classical way, backward: take the parametric smiles already fitted, differentiate them, and divide. The result is called the Dupire twin, and the tab sets it beside the fitted sheet.

The first line. In these coordinates it is the pricing equation of two slides back, solved for the local variance. That is the time derivative of the call, over one half x squared times its second strike derivative. The numerator is a calendar spread, the denominator a butterfly, that is, the density. In total variance it is Gatheral's formula: the time derivative of total variance over the butterfly function g. The app builds the total variance from the displayed parametric fits, at the spot they were calibrated at. Between expiries it interpolates in tau, through zero at tau zero, with a monotone cubic, the Smooth chip, or linearly, the Buckets chip. The Tails chips set the twin beyond each expiry's quoted range: the model's own wings by default, held flat from the quoted edge, or the fitted sheet. It differentiates by finite differences and counts every repair. A cell with g at or below zero is a butterfly arbitrage of the parametric surface itself; a cell with falling total variance is a calendar arbitrage. Floored and capped cells are counted too.

Why this direction is delicate. Differentiation amplifies noise, twice in strike and once in time, and the denominator is a density, small in the wings. Starting from smooth parametric smiles keeps it usable. But the twin inherits every choice of that surface: its interpolation in time, its tails, any arbitrage it carries.

The twin is then repriced through the same forward equation, on the fit's own lattice made four times finer in strike and eight times finer in time, with a second-order scheme. The second line is the round trip: the RMS gap between the twin's repriced vols and its own parametric source, at the quoted strikes. If differentiation and repricing were exact it would be zero.

Two controls sit beside it. Floor: a flat sheet at the ladder's median implied variance, marched on the same operator. Its exact answer is known, so its error is the operator's own, and no round trip can be read below it. Sheet: the twin sampled only at the fit's vertices, interpolated on triangles like the fitted sheet, and repriced.

The capture: QQQ, the 18 December expiry, haircut target. The three curves sit on top of each other. The row reads parametric 2 basis points, twin 4, affine sheet 2, and 8 on the finer lattice. The round trip is 0.3 bp over a floor of 0.1. The telling number is the last one: the smooth twin, sampled at the vertices, reprices 71 bp away from its source. So the vertex values of a good sheet are not samples of the true local variance. They are the values that make the triangulated sheet price right. That is what the direct fit of the previous slide solves for, and why it exists.

The affine columns. rms is measured on the lattice the fit used; conv reprices the same sheet on a lattice twice as fine in strike and four times as fine in time. The SPY record of 23 September: 3.61 vol bp on the fit's lattice, 5.12 on the finer one, 24.8 at the worst quote. Why show both: an optimiser facing a fixed lattice can bend the vertices to cancel that lattice's own error, so its own residual flatters it. Only another lattice exposes that part.

Two practical points. The comparison is anchored at the calibration spot, so a spot tick does not rebuild the twin. And the Sheets and Difference views need the displayed fit on the same vertex grid as the twin. In the capture it was not, so the difference was withheld until the next Calibrate.
Transition: that closes local volatility. The next section is about time itself: the event-weighted variance clock tau that every equation here has run on.

If asked why not use the twin as the local-volatility surface: it inherits the interpolation and the tails of the parametric surface. It needs repairs wherever that surface carries arbitrage, and its vertex samples reprice poorly. It is a diagnostic. A cold fit does start from the same classical reading, as a starting point only.

If asked whether the finer-lattice number is exact: no. It is the same sheet on a finer lattice, marched with implicit Euler steps. On a flat 15 percent sheet over the SPY ladder, that reprice itself reads 1 to 4 bp at the money. The gap between the two numbers signals discretisation; it is not the exact error.
